body:
So the decision we're making here is to no longer promote return types of functions, and instead always rely on the literal declaration? I'm not certain that produces better behavior.

Example 1 degrades from an analysis error to a runtime error (depending on use, anyway, which is more concerning). So that feels like worse behavior.

Example 2 (as the general case) is more interesting. Is it spelled out anywhere that we have to maintain a function's return type as `Variant` if unspecified, or are we at liberty to promote it? Assuming we're at liberty, I think it would be "better" behavior to automatically promoted to `ANNOTATED_INFERRED` with whatever the type join is of all return paths. That might end up being `Variant` anyway, but it means we can do _better_ than `Variant` in most cases.
___
Another interesting tidbit (which... maybe indicates a bug somewhere else?) is that, with this change, if you try to declare an inferred variable like so:  
```gdscript
var _prop: int

func get_f():
	return _prop

func test():
	var k := get_f() # Illegal, but editor shows `k` as type `int` [from `get_f()`]
```

Then the editor-shown type of `k` is still whatever the inferred type of `get_f()` would have been.

> So the decision we're making here is to no longer promote return types of functions

This never was a supported feature in the first place. A function without specified return type [has an implicit variant return type](https://github.com/HolonProduction/godot/blob/d488d11119b4e0c67619b0c720d7c335ad2d0565/modules/gdscript/gdscript_analyzer.cpp#L1861-L1870). This might be a bit confusing because we are ignoring a typed return in this PR, what's important is the timing. The variant type gets set while resolving the interface of the function. The typed soft type only gets set [after the body of the function was resolved](https://github.com/HolonProduction/godot/blob/d488d11119b4e0c67619b0c720d7c335ad2d0565/modules/gdscript/gdscript_analyzer.cpp#L2051).

So in general when analyzing function bodies we only have the variant type. The blast radius of this soft type is limited to stuff that gets resolved after the body of the function. Consistently that's only setter and getter checks. There might also be some very brittle behaviour based on function order, since functions bodies before the function in question will just see the variant type, while functions after that see the soft-type. We can deal with issues from that if they arise, but in general this PR has no impact on that.

> Example 1 degrades from an analysis error to a runtime error

Fair, but the untyped function is a boundary that the analyzer should not overstep. We are not trying to solve the halting problem here. It's also pretty insignificant, since mixing a typed variable with an untyped getter is an anti pattern. We should just add a warning for it, it is certainly not worth all the complexity we have around this right now.

> Example 2 (as the general case) is more interesting. Is it spelled out anywhere that we have to maintain a function's return type as Variant if unspecified

The best we got is the comment from above, the docs don't make an explicit statement afaik. But the fact that a function without specified return type has an implicit `Variant` return type, is something I've seen as a common sentiment from users. A lot of code operates under that assumption as well.

> Then the editor-shown type of `k` is still whatever the inferred type of `get_f()` would have been.

Since it's a local variable it's probably using the separate type resolution which powers auto completion. That one has very basic control flow analysis, so it might be able to infer the type in this specific case. Not related to this PR though, it's the same without it.

> Fair, but the untyped function is a boundary that the analyzer should not overstep.

Why not? In the event that we _can_ determine a function's return type, elevating it is strictly beneficial to both static analysis and potential optimizations.

> We are not trying to solve the halting problem here.

We don't need to. It's completely within our ability for the analyzer to say "I can't figure out what the return type might be" and degrade to `Variant`. But we should consider the inferred `Variant` as the "worst" resolution we can provide.

> Why not? In the event that we _can_ determine a function's return type, elevating it is strictly beneficial to both static analysis and potential optimizations.

Because the function is virtual and thus all conclusions you make based on this soft type are not generally true.

I'd love to give you an actual crashing code example on that, but I can't because this is not something we do at the moment. This one check for validity of setters/getters is afaik the only code using that soft-type.

If you are talking about some proper return type inference then this would have language design implications because the inferred type would take part in override validation. I personally consider that bad language design, but anyhow this is proposal stuff and I don't want this PR to become a discussion place for return type inference.

__tl;dr__
- For the specific error in the context of this PR a warning on mixing typed vars with untyped getters achieves the same thing in a less convoluted way (the end goal here is to get rid of soft types, in case that wasn't clear)
- For return type inference: please search the proposals repo
Can't exactly blame this one on the core type system though. Soft types are GDScript concoction :mage_man:
I added a warning about the mixing typed/untyped setters and vars to substitute the error that this PR removed: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/123321
